content: Good adherence to antiretroviral therapy (ART) is critical for achieving effective suppression of HIV viral load, which in turn reduces the risk of disease progression and transmission. Accurate methods to monitor adherence are essential, as they can help identify individuals who may benefit from targeted adherence support interventions, particularly in resource-limited settings. The objective of this study was to evaluate the accuracy of simple adherence measures, such as patient self-reports, tablet counts, pharmacy records, electronic monitoring, or composite methods, in detecting non-suppressed viral loads among people living with HIV who are receiving ART. The reference standard used was a viral load assay with detection limits ranging from 10 to 400 copies/mL. The search for relevant studies was comprehensive, covering multiple databases and trial registries up to April 22, 2021, without restrictions on language or publication date. Studies of all designs were included if they evaluated simple adherence measures in people living with HIV on ART. Data were extracted, and the risk of bias was assessed using the QUADAS-2 tool. The certainty of evidence was evaluated using the GRADE approach. A total of 51 studies conducted between 2003 and 2021 were included, involving both children and adults with HIV, primarily from lowand middle-income countries. Many studies assessed more than one adherence measure. The findings for each adherence measure were as follows: Self-reported adherence (25 studies, 9211 participants): Sensitivity ranged from 10% to 85%, and specificity ranged from 10% to 99%. The certainty of evidence was very low. Self-reported adherence using a visual analogue scale (VAS) (11 studies, 4235 participants): Sensitivity ranged from 0% to 58%, and specificity ranged from 55% to 100%. The certainty of evidence was very low. Tablet counts (12 studies, 3466 participants): Sensitivity ranged from 0% to 100%, and specificity ranged from 5% to 99%. The certainty of evidence was very low. Electronic monitoring devices (3 studies, 186 participants): Sensitivity ranged from 60% to 88%, and specificity ranged from 27% to 67%. The certainty of evidence was very low. Pharmacy records or secondary databases (6 studies, 2254 participants): Sensitivity ranged from 17% to 88%, and specificity ranged from 9% to 95%. The certainty of evidence was very low. Composite measures (9 studies, 1513 participants): Sensitivity ranged from 10% to 100%, and specificity ranged from 49% to 100%. The certainty of evidence was very low. Across all studies, there was substantial variability in the sensitivity and specificity of adherence measures for detecting viral non-suppression. This variability could not be adequately explained by subgroup analyses. The overall certainty of evidence was rated as very low due to concerns about risk of bias, indirectness, inconsistency, and imprecision. Methodological issues, such as missing data and unclear reporting, were common. The authors concluded that none of the adherence measures consistently demonstrated high sensitivity or specificity for detecting viral non-suppression. This limits their utility in triaging patients for viral load monitoring or enhanced adherence support interventions. The high variability and low certainty of evidence highlight the need for improved methods to monitor ART adherence effectively.
